headline: Bass gone nocturnal, bluefish picking up the slack — Mattituck to the Gut
subhead: Warm water's pushed the stripers into the dark hours, but the bluefish, fluke, and porgy never got the memo.
body_markdown:
Had a fella pull his skiff up alongside mine off Rocky Point Sunday, must've been eleven in the morning, sun already high and mean. He'd been trolling bunker spoons since seven with nothing to show but a sunburn and a bad attitude. Asked me where the bass were. I told him the truth — they're home. Sleeping it off. Come back at nine tonight and fish the same water and you'll think somebody flipped a switch. He didn't believe me. Most guys that age don't, not till they've fished the Sound sixty summers like I have and watched this exact thing happen every August since Nixon was in office.

Water's sitting in the low seventies right along our stretch — Kings Point's reading just under 71, New London's holding around 69 and a half, which tells you the whole Sound west to east is one long warm bathtub right now with barely a degree of relief anywhere. That's not fish-killing warm, but it's warm enough that a striped bass with any sense at all isn't going to burn calories chasing bait in broad daylight when the water's comfortable and slow-moving all night long. We flagged this pattern last week — said the mid-70s temps would keep bass a low-light player here, and that's exactly the hand we've been dealt. Daytime, they're down deep off the drop-offs by Horton Point and Rocky Point, sulking in whatever cooler water they can find, maybe forty, fifty feet down. Come dusk, they slide up onto the structure and start working the current edges, and that's your window.

Best bass action I've heard of or had myself has come after dark off Horton Point, drifting bunker chunks on fishfinder rigs right along the rock pile where the bottom breaks from hard to soft. Eels fished slow on a slight drift have taken a few keepers too, nothing spectacular, mostly high twenties to low thirties inches, a slot fish here and there mixed with fish you've got to let swim. Plum Gut approach has been holding some better-grade stripers on the tail of the ebb when that current really starts ripping — that's a spot where I tell people bring your heaviest bucktail, three-quarter to full ounce, and let it get down into the rip before you start working it. Current there doesn't forgive a light head. But even at the Gut, it's mostly a dawn-and-dusk game right now, not a two-in-the-afternoon game.

What's making up for the bass going quiet is the bluefish, and they have been dependable in a way the stripers haven't. There's a push of them coming down out of the western Sound right now, and it's spilling into our water — fish mixed in size, a lot of two and three pounders but enough five- and six-pound choppers mixed in to keep your arm sore. They've been thick off Mattituck Inlet on the outgoing, blitzing bunker pods right at the mouth, and a few boats have found them stacked up off Rocky Point too. Nothing fancy needed — a diamond jig or a topwater popper thrown into a working school will get bit fast. Just watch your fingers around the release, these are fresh, aggressive fish, not the lazy resident blues we sometimes get late season.

Fluke's been the steady eddy in all this, same as we said it would be. Sandy patches adjacent to the reef structure off Mattituck and out toward Rocky Point have been giving up a consistent mix of keepers and shorts on the drift — white Gulp Swimming Mullets on half-ounce bucktails, sometimes tipped with a strip of squid if the current's really moving. Nobody's filling a cooler in an hour, but if you work three or four drifts over the right bottom you'll put a few keeper fluke in the boat, four to six pounds on the better ones. It's a patient man's bite, not a blitz, and that's fine by me — I never trusted the blitz bite anyway, it never lasts.

Porgy fishing continues to be what it always is out here — unglamorous, reliable, and a good way to keep the kids interested while you wait for the sun to drop and the real bass window to open. Anywhere there's structure between Mattituck and Orient, a bit of clam on a hi-lo rig will get you bites all afternoon. Blackfish season's still closed in our waters till fall, so leave the tog gear home for now.

Looking ahead, the tide's building toward stronger pushes over the next several days, and that extra current should sharpen up both the Plum Gut bass bite and the bluefish blitzes at the inlets — moving water concentrates the bait, and concentrated bait is what turns a so-so evening into a good one. I wouldn't expect any albie or bonito showing this far up the Sound yet — that push tends to hit Montauk and the Race first and take its time working west to us, if it comes at all this early. If I only had one evening to fish this week, I'd be at Horton Point an hour before dark with bunker chunks and eels both rigged and ready, and I'd stay till the tide turned.
